## Target Venue

## Canonical Experimental Condition

**Continuation mode 是 cross-model 结论的基础。**

> "We evaluate both generation modes because real-world recursive contamination can arise from either. Our analysis reveals generation mode as a significant confound, leading us to recommend continuation mode as the canonical condition for cross-model comparisons."

| Condition | Pythia↔OLMo | Qwen↔others | 论文定位 |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|---------|
| Continuation | 90-92% retention | 80-85% retention | **主实验条件** — cross-model claims 的基础 |
| Rewrite (instruction) | N/A | 61-63% retention | **upper bound with mode-specific confound** — 仅作 ablation |

- C1' 的跨模型 claim 必须基于 continuation mode 数据

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
5	Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
6	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
7	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
8	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
9	Further work shows that even a vanishingly small fraction of synthetic data suffices to trigger collapse, with the effect amplified in larger models~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}.
10	Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
11	Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
12	Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
13	Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
14	Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
15	Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} proved that collapse is avoidable when sufficient original data is retained alongside synthetic samples, a condition that depth-aware curation can enforce by construction.
16	These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.
17	
18	\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
19	Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
20	Early statistical approaches such as GLTR~\cite{gehrmann2019gltr} visualized per-token likelihood ranks to help human annotators spot generated text, establishing that token-level distributional cues are informative for detection.
21	Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
22	Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
23	Fast-DetectGPT~\citep{bao2024fast} dramatically accelerates this approach via conditional probability curvature, achieving a 340$\times$ speedup with improved accuracy.
24	Hans et al.~\cite{hans2024binoculars} proposed Binoculars, which computes the cross-perplexity ratio between two closely related language models to achieve near-perfect detection without any training data.
25	DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
26	CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.
27	
28	All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
29	The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
30	A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
31	Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.
32	
33	\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
34	Ordinal regression methods exploit the natural ordering among class labels to improve generalization over nominal classifiers.
35	Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
36	Ordinal approaches have been applied in NLP tasks such as sentiment intensity prediction and essay scoring, where adjacent categories share more semantic overlap than distant ones.
37	Generational depth exhibits the same ordinal structure: text at depth~$k$ is distributionally closer to depth~$k\!\pm\!1$ than to depth~$k\!\pm\!3$, because each recursive generation step introduces an incremental distributional shift rather than a discontinuous one.
38	Despite this natural fit, ordinal classification has not been applied to synthetic text depth estimation.
39	The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.
40	
41	\paragraph{Probing Classifiers.}
42	Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
43	Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
44	Our neural probe experiment follows this protocol: a two-layer MLP on frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings, where the probe's limited capacity ensures that discriminability reflects depth information already present in the representations rather than learned de novo.
45	
46	\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
47	Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
48	DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
49	D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Further work shows that even a vanishingly small fraction of synthetic data suffices to trigger collapse, with the effect amplified in larger models~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}.
Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} proved that collapse is avoidable when sufficient original data is retained alongside synthetic samples, a condition that depth-aware curation can enforce by construction.
These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.

\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
Early statistical approaches such as GLTR~\cite{gehrmann2019gltr} visualized per-token likelihood ranks to help human annotators spot generated text, establishing that token-level distributional cues are informative for detection.
Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
Fast-DetectGPT~\citep{bao2024fast} dramatically accelerates this approach via conditional probability curvature, achieving a 340$\times$ speedup with improved accuracy.
Hans et al.~\cite{hans2024binoculars} proposed Binoculars, which computes the cross-perplexity ratio between two closely related language models to achieve near-perfect detection without any training data.
DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.

All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
Ordinal regression methods exploit the natural ordering among class labels to improve generalization over nominal classifiers.
Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
Ordinal approaches have been applied in NLP tasks such as sentiment intensity prediction and essay scoring, where adjacent categories share more semantic overlap than distant ones.
Generational depth exhibits the same ordinal structure: text at depth~$k$ is distributionally closer to depth~$k\!\pm\!1$ than to depth~$k\!\pm\!3$, because each recursive generation step introduces an incremental distributional shift rather than a discontinuous one.
Despite this natural fit, ordinal classification has not been applied to synthetic text depth estimation.
The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.

\paragraph{Probing Classifiers.}
Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
Our neural probe experiment follows this protocol: a two-layer MLP on frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings, where the probe's limited capacity ensures that discriminability reflects depth information already present in the representations rather than learned de novo.

\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
These methods operate on distributional properties of the corpus but do not estimate whether individual documents have undergone recursive generation.

The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
Their approach is a special case of our graduated filtering framework: when $\Kstar = 1$, ordinal depth estimation reduces to binary classification, and depth-aware curation degenerates to their SIR-based scheme.
We generalize this binary formulation to ordinal depth estimation, enabling finer-grained curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$).
Recent work demonstrates that external verification can prevent model collapse during recursive training~\citep{feng2025beyond}, positioning depth estimation as a natural verification signal for data curation.
Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.

\paragraph{Watermarking and Provenance.}
An alternative approach embeds identifiers at generation time.
Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.
Watermarking is complementary to depth estimation: it requires control over the generation process and cooperation from providers, whereas our method operates post-hoc on unwatermarked text.
The two approaches address different threat models---watermarking assumes a cooperative generator, while depth estimation targets uncontrolled settings where provenance metadata is unavailable.

6:Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
7:Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
8:Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
10:Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
12:Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
14:Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
15:Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} proved that collapse is avoidable when sufficient original data is retained alongside synthetic samples, a condition that depth-aware curation can enforce by construction.
20:Early statistical approaches such as GLTR~\cite{gehrmann2019gltr} visualized per-token likelihood ranks to help human annotators spot generated text, establishing that token-level distributional cues are informative for detection.
21:Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
22:Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
24:Hans et al.~\cite{hans2024binoculars} proposed Binoculars, which computes the cross-perplexity ratio between two closely related language models to achieve near-perfect detection without any training data.
25:DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
26:CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.
35:Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
39:The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.
42:Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
43:Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
48:DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
49:D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
52:The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
56:Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
57:Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.
61:Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
5	\label{sec:discuss_kstar}
6	
7	The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
8	Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations and 4 decoding strategies; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.
9	
10	The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
11	The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
12	At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; see also Figure~\ref{fig:s1_auc_decay_ci} in the Appendix), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
13	By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions (upper bound from nucleus $p{=}0.9$ decoding; Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
14	Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.
15	
16	The feature degradation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides mechanistic evidence for this rapid collapse.
17	The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
18	Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
19	The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
20	Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs; Table~\ref{tab:top_features}), suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the autoregressive generation mechanism itself rather than by model-specific biases.
21	
22	This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
23	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
24	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
25	Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
26	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.
27	
28	Importantly, $\Kempirical = 2$ is an \emph{operational} lower bound conditioned on the 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set; the \emph{theoretical} boundary $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.
29	Preliminary evidence from a neural probing experiment supports this distinction.
30	A frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder (1536-dimensional last-layer representations) paired with a lightweight MLP classifier (Table~\ref{tab:s7_neural_probe}) achieves 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$) on the Qwen-continuation dataset, exceeding the $\theta = 0.60$ threshold that the same dataset's LightGBM classifier fails to cross ($\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
31	This yields $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$: the learned representation recovers one additional discriminable boundary that the hand-crafted features miss.
32	The improvement is concentrated at the 2v3 pair ($+$5.86\,pp over LightGBM); at the already-separable 1v2 boundary the neural probe achieves 0.6983 versus 0.6112, a substantial gain but one that does not alter the boundary determination.
33	At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any hand-crafted configuration---suggesting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.
34	The lossy-channel narrative remains intact: even with 1536-dimensional frozen representations, the discrimination boundary extends to only three steps, confirming that the information bottleneck of recursive generation is shallow even with substantially richer representations.
35	These results are preliminary: they cover a single model-dataset pair (Qwen-continuation) and lack bootstrap confidence intervals; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.
36	
37	The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
38	Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
39	Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
40	This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.
41	
42	\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
43	\label{sec:discuss_transfer}
44	
45	The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
46	Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs (Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix}; see Table~\ref{tab:s1_transfer} for the full matrix).
47	At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 across all tested model pairs, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across the tested generators.
48	
49	The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
50	This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.
51	
52	Two caveats bound this conclusion.
53	First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
54	The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
55	Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.
56	
57	\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
58	\label{sec:discuss_features}
59	
60	While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
61	Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
62	In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
63	Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.
64	
65	This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
66	High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
67	For practitioners, this implies that a general-purpose depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.
68	
69	The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
70	A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.
71	
72	\subsection{Scale Considerations}
73	\label{sec:discuss_scale}
74	
75	Our experiments establish $\Kempirical = 2$ at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale, providing the first empirical measurement of the generational depth boundary for language models.
76	This result constitutes a \emph{methodological lower bound}: the framework itself---15-dimensional token-level features, OBD-optimized classification, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation testing---is model-scale agnostic by construction.
77	All 15 features are computed from surface-level token statistics (surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, frequency tail measures) without access to model internals, and the cross-model transfer results (80--92\% retention across architecturally distinct model families; Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) already demonstrate that the methodology generalizes across different architectures and training corpora at the tested scale.
78	
79	Scaling to larger models presents two possible outcomes, both of which reinforce rather than diminish the contribution.
80	If $\Kempirical > 2$ at 7B+ scales---as suggested by scaling laws showing that larger models exhibit slower tail-distribution degradation rates~\cite{dohmatob2024model, kaplan2020scaling}---then depth contamination becomes \emph{more} insidious: higher-fidelity generations would produce weaker depth signatures, making fine-grained detection more critical and the systematic framework we introduce more necessary.
81	Conversely, if $\Kempirical = 2$ persists at larger scales, our conclusions generalize directly.
82	In either case, the measurement methodology established here---the feature taxonomy, the $\Kstar$ estimation protocol, and the cross-model validation framework---provides the requisite infrastructure for characterizing depth boundaries at any scale.
83	The model collapse literature supports the expectation that depth-related phenomena are scale-persistent: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed tail-mode collapse across model sizes, and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved fixed-point convergence for self-consuming generators without scale-dependent assumptions.
84	
85	We identify 7B-scale cross-scale validation as the immediate next step.
86	The experimental pipeline---data generation, feature extraction, and classifier evaluation---is fully implemented and directly applicable to larger models; only computational budget constrains this extension.
87	Critically, this limitation does not affect the validity of the $\Kempirical = 2$ result at $\leq$1.5B, which stands as the first empirical characterization of generational depth boundaries in language model outputs.
88	
89	\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
90	\label{sec:discuss_llm}
91	
92	Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
93	On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), excluding depth~5 from the 6-class range used in the main feature-based experiments since depths $\geq 3$ are mutually indistinguishable ($\Kempirical = 2$), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11; see Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot} for per-depth confusion matrices).
94	Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).
95	
96	This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
97	Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
98	Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
99	The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
100	This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
101	We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.
102	
103	\subsection{Limitations}
104	\label{sec:limitations}
105	
106	We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.
107	
108	\emph{Model scale.}
109	All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
110	Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.
111	
112	\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
113	Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
114	Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
115	Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.
116	
117	\emph{Language and domain.}
118	All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
119	Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.
120	
121	\emph{Decoding coverage.}
122	We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
123	Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.
124	
125	\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
126	$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
127	$\Kempirical \geq 2$ across $\theta \in \{0.55, 0.60, 0.65\}$ for all four decoding strategies, rising to $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$ (all four 2v3 $\auc$ values exceed 0.55) and returning to $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\theta \in \{0.60, 0.65\}$.
128	At $\theta = 0.70$, three of four decoding configurations collapse to $\Kempirical = 1$; only the high-temperature setting ($T{=}1.2$) retains $\Kempirical = 2$, consistent with its elevated 1v2 $\auc$ (0.7039).
129	Beyond decoding parameters, the threshold sensitivity extends to generation mode: at $\theta{=}0.70$, $\Kempirical{=}1$ for all four model-mode configurations; at $\theta{=}0.65$, continuation-mode configurations already drop to $\Kempirical{=}1$, while rewrite mode retains $\Kempirical{=}2$.
130	Our current analysis primarily covers the decoding configuration axis.
131	The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.
132	
133	\emph{Boundary marginality.}
134	The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
135	On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
136	On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
137	This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary---as the neural probe results confirm, where a richer representation pushes the 2v3 pair above $\theta$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}).
138	Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.
139	
140	\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
141	$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
142	$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.
143	Preliminary neural probing results provide direct evidence for this gap: on the Qwen-continuation dataset, a frozen-encoder MLP achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$) compared to $\Kempirical = 2$ with 15-dimensional hand-crafted features (2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
144	This confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal and that $\Ktheory \geq 3$.
145	However, the neural probe result rests on a single dataset and awaits cross-model validation and bootstrap confidence intervals before a firm revision of the headline $\Kempirical$ can be claimed.
146	
147	\emph{Feature representation.}
148	The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is not optimal.
149	A preliminary neural probing experiment demonstrates that frozen LLM embeddings (1536 dimensions) paired with a lightweight MLP push $\Kempirical$ from~2 to~3 on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}), confirming that learned representations capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss.
150	The magnitude of the gain---2v3 $\auc$ rising from 0.5609 to 0.6195---indicates meaningful recoverable signal beyond what hand-crafted features extract.
151	Full characterization of this gap, including cross-model generalization and bootstrap uncertainty quantification, remains future work.
152	
153	\paragraph{Graduated Filtering.}
154	Results for graduated filtering will be added upon completion of ongoing experiments.
155	
156	\subsection{Broader Impact}
157	\label{sec:broader_impact}
158	
159	The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.
160	
161	\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
162	The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
163	Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
164	For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
165	This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
166	Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.
167	
168	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
169	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
170	Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
171	The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
172	If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.
173	
174	\paragraph{AI text detection.}
175	Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
176	Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
177	The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
\label{sec:discuss_kstar}

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations and 4 decoding strategies; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.

The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; see also Figure~\ref{fig:s1_auc_decay_ci} in the Appendix), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions (upper bound from nucleus $p{=}0.9$ decoding; Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.

The feature degradation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides mechanistic evidence for this rapid collapse.
The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs; Table~\ref{tab:top_features}), suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the autoregressive generation mechanism itself rather than by model-specific biases.

This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

Importantly, $\Kempirical = 2$ is an \emph{operational} lower bound conditioned on the 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set; the \emph{theoretical} boundary $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.
Preliminary evidence from a neural probing experiment supports this distinction.
A frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder (1536-dimensional last-layer representations) paired with a lightweight MLP classifier (Table~\ref{tab:s7_neural_probe}) achieves 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$) on the Qwen-continuation dataset, exceeding the $\theta = 0.60$ threshold that the same dataset's LightGBM classifier fails to cross ($\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
This yields $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$: the learned representation recovers one additional discriminable boundary that the hand-crafted features miss.
The improvement is concentrated at the 2v3 pair ($+$5.86\,pp over LightGBM); at the already-separable 1v2 boundary the neural probe achieves 0.6983 versus 0.6112, a substantial gain but one that does not alter the boundary determination.
At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any hand-crafted configuration---suggesting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.
The lossy-channel narrative remains intact: even with 1536-dimensional frozen representations, the discrimination boundary extends to only three steps, confirming that the information bottleneck of recursive generation is shallow even with substantially richer representations.
These results are preliminary: they cover a single model-dataset pair (Qwen-continuation) and lack bootstrap confidence intervals; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.

The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.

\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:discuss_transfer}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs (Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix}; see Table~\ref{tab:s1_transfer} for the full matrix).
At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 across all tested model pairs, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across the tested generators.

The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.

Two caveats bound this conclusion.
First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
\label{sec:discuss_features}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.

This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
For practitioners, this implies that a general-purpose depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.

The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.

\subsection{Scale Considerations}
\label{sec:discuss_scale}

Our experiments establish $\Kempirical = 2$ at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale, providing the first empirical measurement of the generational depth boundary for language models.
This result constitutes a \emph{methodological lower bound}: the framework itself---15-dimensional token-level features, OBD-optimized classification, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation testing---is model-scale agnostic by construction.
All 15 features are computed from surface-level token statistics (surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, frequency tail measures) without access to model internals, and the cross-model transfer results (80--92\% retention across architecturally distinct model families; Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) already demonstrate that the methodology generalizes across different architectures and training corpora at the tested scale.

Scaling to larger models presents two possible outcomes, both of which reinforce rather than diminish the contribution.
If $\Kempirical > 2$ at 7B+ scales---as suggested by scaling laws showing that larger models exhibit slower tail-distribution degradation rates~\cite{dohmatob2024model, kaplan2020scaling}---then depth contamination becomes \emph{more} insidious: higher-fidelity generations would produce weaker depth signatures, making fine-grained detection more critical and the systematic framework we introduce more necessary.
Conversely, if $\Kempirical = 2$ persists at larger scales, our conclusions generalize directly.
In either case, the measurement methodology established here---the feature taxonomy, the $\Kstar$ estimation protocol, and the cross-model validation framework---provides the requisite infrastructure for characterizing depth boundaries at any scale.
The model collapse literature supports the expectation that depth-related phenomena are scale-persistent: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed tail-mode collapse across model sizes, and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved fixed-point convergence for self-consuming generators without scale-dependent assumptions.

We identify 7B-scale cross-scale validation as the immediate next step.
The experimental pipeline---data generation, feature extraction, and classifier evaluation---is fully implemented and directly applicable to larger models; only computational budget constrains this extension.
Critically, this limitation does not affect the validity of the $\Kempirical = 2$ result at $\leq$1.5B, which stands as the first empirical characterization of generational depth boundaries in language model outputs.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:discuss_llm}

Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), excluding depth~5 from the 6-class range used in the main feature-based experiments since depths $\geq 3$ are mutually indistinguishable ($\Kempirical = 2$), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11; see Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot} for per-depth confusion matrices).
Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).

This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.

\emph{Model scale.}
All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.

\emph{Language and domain.}
All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.

\emph{Decoding coverage.}
We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
$\Kempirical \geq 2$ across $\theta \in \{0.55, 0.60, 0.65\}$ for all four decoding strategies, rising to $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$ (all four 2v3 $\auc$ values exceed 0.55) and returning to $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\theta \in \{0.60, 0.65\}$.

Beyond decoding parameters, the threshold sensitivity extends to generation mode: at $\theta{=}0.70$, $\Kempirical{=}1$ for all four model-mode configurations; at $\theta{=}0.65$, continuation-mode configurations already drop to $\Kempirical{=}1$, while rewrite mode retains $\Kempirical{=}2$.
Our current analysis primarily covers the decoding configuration axis.
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary---as the neural probe results confirm, where a richer representation pushes the 2v3 pair above $\theta$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}).
Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.

\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.
Preliminary neural probing results provide direct evidence for this gap: on the Qwen-continuation dataset, a frozen-encoder MLP achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$) compared to $\Kempirical = 2$ with 15-dimensional hand-crafted features (2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
This confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal and that $\Ktheory \geq 3$.
However, the neural probe result rests on a single dataset and awaits cross-model validation and bootstrap confidence intervals before a firm revision of the headline $\Kempirical$ can be claimed.

\emph{Feature representation.}
The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is not optimal.
A preliminary neural probing experiment demonstrates that frozen LLM embeddings (1536 dimensions) paired with a lightweight MLP push $\Kempirical$ from~2 to~3 on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}), confirming that learned representations capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss.
The magnitude of the gain---2v3 $\auc$ rising from 0.5609 to 0.6195---indicates meaningful recoverable signal beyond what hand-crafted features extract.
Full characterization of this gap, including cross-model generalization and bootstrap uncertainty quantification, remains future work.

\paragraph{Graduated Filtering.}
Results for graduated filtering will be added upon completion of ongoing experiments.

\subsection{Broader Impact}
\label{sec:broader_impact}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.

\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.

\paragraph{AI text detection.}
Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Each pass through a language model constitutes a lossy channel: first-generation synthetic text retains much of the information structure of its human-written source, but within just two or three generations the output is qualitatively different---tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This recursive degradation is not merely a theoretical concern; as synthetic text proliferates on the open web, training corpora inevitably ingest documents at varying generational depths, amplifying the risk of model collapse in downstream systems.
Yet the dominant paradigm in synthetic text detection treats all machine-generated text identically: a document is classified as human or synthetic, with no regard for how many rounds of recursive generation it has undergone.
This binary framing discards the generational depth dimension entirely.

The gap cuts across three research communities.
Binary detection methods---including DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye}, Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp}, and CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec}---achieve strong human-versus-machine separation but produce no depth estimate.
The model collapse literature provides macro-level characterizations of recursive degradation: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} demonstrated irreversible tail loss, Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point, and Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the field into a taxonomy of eight definitions---yet none of these works provides a tool for estimating the generational depth of an individual text.
Data selection methods such as DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir}, D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4}, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} perform distribution matching to improve corpus quality but ignore recursive depth altogether.
The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling to prevent model collapse---but their approach remains fundamentally binary.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone, nor quantifies the boundary beyond which such estimation becomes infeasible.

Recursive generation forms an iterated lossy channel; the Data Processing Inequality guarantees that the original signal degrades monotonically across generations, motivating the existence of a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable.
Markov chain convergence further implies that adjacent-generation distributions converge to a shared stationary distribution, so the classifier's task grows harder with each step.
Motivated by this theoretical structure, we set out to empirically measure $\Kempirical$---the maximum depth at which a classifier can reliably distinguish adjacent generations.
Our approach combines a 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline---capturing surprisal moments, surprisal derivatives, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---with an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier that respects the ordinal structure of depth.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest generation at which adjacent depths remain statistically distinguishable, with the bootstrap 95\% CI for pairwise $\auc$ exceeding an operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (formal definition in Section~\ref{sec:method}).
The choice of interpretable statistical features---rather than learned representations---is deliberate: it enables cross-generator transfer without retraining and permits attribution of discriminative power to specific text properties.

Our contributions are organized into two groups.
The primary contribution is a systematic empirical characterization of $\Kempirical$ and its properties:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item \textbf{$\Kempirical = 2$: a consistent boundary across all tested conditions.}
    Across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total), all 1v2 bootstrap CI lower bounds exceed $\theta = 0.60$ and all 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$, with permutation $p \leq 0.002$ for all boundary comparisons.
    The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where $\text{CI}_\text{lower} = 0.6015$.
    $\Kempirical = 2$ is thus established as a consistent discrimination boundary across all 8 tested conditions at the $\leq$1.5B scale.
    Higher decoding entropy increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: $0.69$ greedy $\to$ $0.70$ at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.

  \item \textbf{Cross-model transfer.}
    Classifiers trained on one continuation-mode model and evaluated on another retain 80--92\% of within-model accuracy (Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo: 90--92\%).
    At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 across all tested model pairs.
    Transfer retention of 80--92\% suggests a large text-intrinsic component of the depth signal, rather than generator-specific artifacts.

  \item \textbf{Degradation ordering consistency.}
    Single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly correlated across continuation-mode models (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with the same top features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---appearing across all three families.
    This shared ordering suggests a common degradation mechanism: each generation step smooths the token-level surprisal landscape.
    A limitation is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens ($\tau \approx 0.37$ at 1v2), indicating that individual feature contributions at the boundary vary across models.

  \item \textbf{Generation mode analysis.}
    Within Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, rewrite mode yields 1v2 $\auc = 0.6955$ versus continuation's $0.6112$ ($\Delta = +8.4$\,pp), but rewrite-trained classifiers transfer poorly across models (61--63\% retention versus 80--92\% for continuation).
    Cross-mode transfer is asymmetric: continuation$\to$rewrite retains 89\% while rewrite$\to$continuation retains 82\%.
    Continuation mode is therefore recommended as the canonical condition for cross-model comparisons.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a secondary contribution, we investigate whether the coarse 3-class ordinal signal implied by $\Kempirical = 2$ enables \emph{graduated filtering}---depth-aware data curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$)---and whether such filtering can improve upon binary approaches that discard all synthetic content indiscriminately (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section~\ref{sec:related_work} reviews related work.
Section~\ref{sec:method} describes the method.
Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents experimental results.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

classifiers reliably distinguish adjacent generations up to depth~2, but all
deeper pairs fall below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$.

($p \leq 0.002$ for all four); the most marginal case, Qwen-continuation,

likewise yield 1v2 point-estimate $\auc$ above $\theta$.

statistical fingerprint is exhausted within two steps.

% === Contribution 2: Ordinal depth estimation framework ===

\subsection{Graduated Filtering for Depth-Aware Data Curation}
\label{sec:graduated-filtering}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary establishes a three-tier taxonomy: human (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Binary filtering discards all synthetic content indiscriminately, sacrificing depth-1 text that retains most of the original signal.
We ask whether exploiting the coarse ordinal structure---weighting samples by predicted depth rather than applying a hard human/synthetic threshold---improves downstream language model quality.

\paragraph{Filtering strategies.}
We compare six data curation strategies applied to a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth level, depths 0--5) produced by the generational depth pipeline:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item \textbf{No-filter}: all documents receive uniform weight (baseline).

  \item \textbf{Binary-ours}: a LightGBM classifier trained on the 15-dimensional feature set distinguishes human (depth~0) from synthetic (depth~$\geq 1$).
  Each document receives weight $w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$.
  This represents the natural binary extension of our depth estimation framework.

  \item \textbf{Binary-Drayson}: stratified importance resampling following Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, with $w_j = (1 - q(x_j))^b / Z$, $b = 1.5$, and oversampling factor $k = 1.5$.
  This is the strongest existing baseline for contamination-aware data curation.

  \item \textbf{Graduated}: our proposed depth-aware strategy.
  The OBD-LightGBM classifier (Section~\ref{sec:classifier}) predicts a full depth distribution $P(d \mid \mathbf{x})$ for each document, from which we compute the expected depth $\hat{d} = \sum_d d \cdot P(d \mid \mathbf{x})$.
  Sample weights follow an exponential decay: $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, where $\alpha$ controls the penalty for predicted depth.
  Low $\alpha$ values retain more synthetic content with gentle down-weighting; high $\alpha$ values approximate hard filtering.
  We sweep $\alpha \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$.

  \item \textbf{Surprisal}: a feature-based heuristic that retains documents whose mean surprisal exceeds the corpus median, exploiting the observation that deeper generations exhibit lower surprisal variance (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}).

  \item \textbf{DSIR}: Data Selection via Importance Resampling~\cite{xie2023dsir}, using bigram feature hashing with the depth-0 subcorpus as the reference distribution.
  This represents the state-of-the-art domain-matching baseline that is agnostic to generational depth.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Training setup.}

Each strategy is evaluated across 5 random seeds (42, 123, 456, 789, 1024); the graduated strategy is further crossed with 5 $\alpha$ values, yielding 25 additional runs.
A base model baseline (no fine-tuning) is included for reference.
The total experimental budget is approximately 50 runs.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We evaluate on two standard benchmarks via lm-eval-harness: MMLU (14{,}042 test examples, 0-shot) and HellaSwag (10{,}042 validation examples, 0-shot).
We report mean accuracy $\pm$ standard deviation across seeds.

\subsection{Scale Considerations}
\label{sec:discuss_scale}

Our experiments establish $\Kempirical = 2$ at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale, providing the first empirical measurement of the generational depth boundary for language models.
This result constitutes a \emph{methodological lower bound}: the framework itself---15-dimensional token-level features, OBD-optimized classification, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation testing---is model-scale agnostic by construction.
All 15 features are computed from surface-level token statistics (surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, frequency tail measures) without access to model internals, and the cross-model transfer results (80--92\% retention across architecturally distinct model families; Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) already demonstrate that the methodology generalizes across different architectures and training corpora at the tested scale.

Scaling to larger models presents two possible outcomes, both of which reinforce rather than diminish the contribution.
If $\Kempirical > 2$ at 7B+ scales---as suggested by scaling laws showing that larger models exhibit slower tail-distribution degradation rates~\cite{dohmatob2024model, kaplan2020scaling}---then depth contamination becomes \emph{more} insidious: higher-fidelity generations would produce weaker depth signatures, making fine-grained detection more critical and the systematic framework we introduce more necessary.
Conversely, if $\Kempirical = 2$ persists at larger scales, our conclusions generalize directly.
In either case, the measurement methodology established here---the feature taxonomy, the $\Kstar$ estimation protocol, and the cross-model validation framework---provides the requisite infrastructure for characterizing depth boundaries at any scale.
The model collapse literature supports the expectation that depth-related phenomena are scale-persistent: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed tail-mode collapse across model sizes, and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved fixed-point convergence for self-consuming generators without scale-dependent assumptions.

We identify 7B-scale cross-scale validation as the immediate next step.
The experimental pipeline---data generation, feature extraction, and classifier evaluation---is fully implemented and directly applicable to larger models; only computational budget constrains this extension.
Critically, this limitation does not affect the validity of the $\Kempirical = 2$ result at $\leq$1.5B, which stands as the first empirical characterization of generational depth boundaries in language model outputs.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:discuss_llm}
